content: During the reporting period, tuberculosis (TB) preventive therapy with isoniazid was emphasized as a critical component of the World Health Organization (WHO) TB/HIV Three I’s strategy. This therapy is a vital part of comprehensive HIV care to prevent TB in individuals living with HIV. WHO strongly recommends a minimum six-month course of TB preventive therapy for all people with HIV, excluding those with presumed or confirmed active TB. In high TB transmission settings, a conditional recommendation is made for extending the therapy to at least 36 months. The indicator for monitoring this intervention has been revised to align with the treat all recommendations, now focusing on individuals started on antiretroviral therapy (ART) rather than those newly enrolled in HIV care. In countries with less than 90% ART coverage among those enrolled in HIV care, patients not yet started on ART (and without active TB) may also be included in the denominator. Additionally, patients who began TB preventive therapy at the time of HIV care enrollment are added to the numerator. Hepatitis C screening is another key area of focus, with indicators disaggregated by sex and age (<15 and 15+ years). Testing involves hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) and hepatitis C virus antibody (HCV Ab) tests, followed by HCV RNA testing for those who test positive for anti-HCV antibodies. ART registers now include specific columns for these indicators, and definitions for numerators and denominators have been updated to reflect newly initiated on ART rather than in HIV care. Adherence to ART is critical for achieving individual and population-level benefits of HIV treatment. The on-time pill pick-up indicator assesses how well patients adhere to their ART schedules by picking up prescribed medications before running out. WHO recommends a target of over 90% for excellent clinic-level performance, with 80–90% considered fair and less than 80% deemed poor. Sustained adherence is essential to prevent virological failure and the emergence of drug-resistant HIV, particularly among individuals on non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NNRTI)-based regimens. However, measuring adherence can be challenging due to the unreliability of self-reported data and provider perceptions. ART toxicity prevalence is monitored as a quality-of-care indicator, measuring the percentage of patients who experience treatment-limiting toxicities. These toxicities are a common reason for poor adherence, treatment discontinuation, or drug substitution. Routine monitoring provides data on the incidence and clinical significance of serious toxicities and their impact on patient outcomes. This indicator is included in the WHO 2015 consolidated guidelines for national program monitoring. Viral load suppression at 12 months is a cohort-based indicator measuring the proportion of patients on ART who achieve viral suppression (<1000 copies/mL). WHO recommends a target of 90% or greater for desirable performance, with 80–90% considered fair and less than 80% poor. This indicator is critical for minimizing HIV-related morbidity and mortality, reducing HIV incidence, and preventing the emergence of drug resistance. Routine patient monitoring systems are used to collect this data, with disaggregation by sex and age. Co-trimoxazole (CTX) prophylaxis is an integral part of HIV care to prevent common co-infections, particularly in settings with high prevalence of malaria and severe bacterial infections. WHO recommends CTX for all HIV-positive adults and children in such settings, as well as for specific populations such as HIV-exposed infants and individuals with advanced HIV disease or active TB. TB screening coverage in HIV care is another critical indicator, measuring the proportion of individuals in HIV care who were screened for TB during the reporting period. WHO recommends intensified case-finding using a simple algorithm based on clinical symptoms to screen all patients at every visit. The use of Xpert MTB/RIF as the initial diagnostic test for TB is strongly recommended for its accuracy in detecting TB and rifampicin resistance. Finally, TB preventive therapy completion is monitored to assess the proportion of individuals living with HIV who complete the course of treatment for latent TB infection. This indicator is essential for evaluating the effectiveness of TB prevention efforts in HIV care settings. Countries with less than 100% ART coverage should include patients who complete TB preventive therapy in their reporting.
